answer.summary: Kevin Weil sees chat as effective because it is a familiar, universal, unstructured way to communicate that can handle a wide range of intentions and intelligence levels. LLMs can understand the nuance that made this interface impractical before; chat is a flexible baseline, though prescribed interfaces can be better for narrower, high-volume tasks.

sections.heading: Why chat fits AI
sections.content: Weil calls chat versatile and universal because it resembles how people already communicate—in speech, face-to-face interaction, or text messaging. Its unstructured nature lets people express more than a rigid interface would, preserving greater communication bandwidth across many kinds of requests. He says this suits models that can understand the complexity and nuance of human speech, something earlier systems could not do well; the interface matches the models’ capabilities.

sections.heading: A flexible baseline, not the only interface
sections.content: Chat offers a no-restrictions, open-ended way to interact, including by speaking rather than typing. Weil does not claim every task is best served by chat: high-volume, prescribed use cases may work better with a less flexible interface optimized for a specific task. He sees chat as the catch-all for anything users may want to express beyond a given vertical’s narrower interface.
